Finding: Availability is not mathematically bounded to 0-100% because MTTR is not guarded against a negative Work-Order duration (CompletionDate < StartDate).
Evidence: ReliabilityService.cs GetEquipmentReliabilityAsync: Availability guard is only `(MTBFHours + MTTRHours) > 0`, with no check on the sign of MTTRHours. ReliabilityDataQualityService.cs already computes FailureRecordsWithNegativeDuration as a separate data-quality metric, confirming the condition is anticipated elsewhere in the codebase but not excluded here. Confirmed by full code read; real-world occurrence NotVerified (0 live FailureRecords in current dev DB).
UserImpact: A user could see an Availability value above 100% or in an unintuitive range for an equipment with a negative-duration linked Work Order, with no on-screen indication anything is wrong.
AnalyticsImpact: Skews the single per-equipment Availability value and, since class-level Availability is a simple average of per-equipment values (see G-4), can propagate into class/fleet rollups.
DataIntegrityImpact: No - a negative-duration WorkOrder is already counted by ReliabilityDataQualityService.FailureRecordsWithNegativeDuration, but that count is not cross-referenced or excluded by ReliabilityService's own calculation, so the two pages can disagree silently.
CurrentWorkaround: None currently - the Reliability page does not warn the user when its own inputs overlap with a known data-quality issue.
RecommendedAction: Exclude (or clamp) failures whose linked WorkOrder has CompletionDate < StartDate from the MTTR average, mirroring the exclusion ReliabilityDataQualityService already flags.
RequiresProductDecision: Yes - decide whether to exclude or clamp
Status: and whether to backfill/flag already-affected records

Finding: FailureRecord.FailureModeId/FailureCauseId (the FK fields the Pareto and taxonomy-coverage queries filter on) are never set by any write path in the codebase, so these two charts and this one KPI are structurally non-functional regardless of data volume.
Evidence: Exhaustive grep across PEMS.Persistence and PEMS.Web for `FailureModeId =` / `FailureCauseId =` shows these are only ever set on FMEAItem (via FMEAService.cs, RcmFmeaReadinessService.cs), never on FailureRecord. WorkOrderLifecycleService.SyncFailureRecordAsync - the sole FailureRecord write path - only sets the free-text FailureMode/FailureCause string fields. GetFailureModeParetoAsync/GetFailureCauseParetoAsync (ReliabilityAnalyticsService.cs) filter on FailureModeRef/FailureCauseRef (FK navigation), and FailureTaxonomyCoveragePercent (ReliabilityDataQualityService.cs) counts FailureModeId==null.
UserImpact: The Failure Mode Pareto chart, Failure Cause Pareto chart, and FailureTaxonomyCoveragePercent indicator will show empty/near-0% results even when the equivalent free-text data (FailureMode/FailureCause strings, correctly used by Bad Actor) is fully populated - a misleading 'no data' or 'always red' appearance.
AnalyticsImpact: Two of the six Reliability Analytics outputs (the Pareto charts) are non-functional; one Data Quality KPI (FailureTaxonomyCoveragePercent) is structurally miscalibrated (reads near-0% independent of actual taxonomy discipline).
DataIntegrityImpact: No - no incorrect data is produced
CurrentWorkaround: the fields are simply always empty/null; this is a completeness gap
RecommendedAction: not a correctness gap on the fields that ARE written.
RequiresCodeChange: None - Bad Actor's PrimaryFailureMode/PrimaryFailureCause (which correctly use the string fields) can substitute as a partial, non-Pareto view of the same underlying information.
RequiresSchemaChange: Either (a) extend SyncFailureRecordAsync to resolve/set FailureModeId/FailureCauseId via a lookup against the FailureMode/FailureCause reference tables by code, or (b) change the two Pareto queries (and the coverage KPI) to group by the existing free-text fields instead of the FK navigation. This is a product/architecture decision, not a pure bug fix - see RequiresProductDecision.
Status: Yes - confirm whether the FK-taxonomy intent (FMEA-aligned) or the free-text intent (as-entered on Work Orders) is the correct long-term source of truth
column16: Yes - which of the two fixes (a) or (b) to pursue

Finding: Deterministic tie-breaking is only two levels deep (FailureCount descending, then TotalDowntimeHours descending); a true three-way tie falls back to LINQ's stable-sort-preserved input order rather than an explicit key such as EquipmentId.
Evidence: Confirmed by full code read of GetBadActorsAsync (ReliabilityAnalyticsService.cs) - no third OrderBy clause exists.
UserImpact: In the rare case of equipment tied on both FailureCount and TotalDowntimeHours, the displayed top-N order/inclusion could vary run-to-run if the underlying query's input ordering is not itself guaranteed stable by the database.
AnalyticsImpact: Marginal - only affects which equipment appears in the very last rank position(s) of a tied top-N cutoff; the ranking of clearly-differentiated Bad Actors is unaffected.
RecommendedAction: Add a final deterministic tie-break key (e.g., EquipmentId ascending) after FailureCount and TotalDowntimeHours.

Finding: GetClassReliabilityAsync computes class-level Availability as a simple average of each equipment's already-computed Availability percentage, not a recomputation from aggregated class-level MTBF/MTTR.
Evidence: Confirmed by full code read: `availabilityValues.Average()` over per-equipment AvailabilityPercent values.
UserImpact: A class containing one equipment with a single low-sample-size 100% Availability value and another with many failures and a lower Availability will show a class average that does not reflect the class's actual aggregate failure/repair experience - equal-weighting regardless of sample size.
AnalyticsImpact: Methodological limitation of the class rollup, not an incorrect per-equipment value; MTBFSampleSize/MTTRSampleSize exist on the DTO and could be used to weight or flag this, but this audit did not confirm (NotVerified) whether the Razor views surface them.
CurrentWorkaround: None currently surfaced to the user beyond whatever the DTO's SampleSize fields could enable if displayed.
RecommendedAction: Either weight the class average by sample size, or clearly label it as a simple average of equipment-level percentages (not a class-level recomputation) in the UI/Help content.
RequiresCodeChange: Optional (UI/Help wording is a non-code fix; a weighted recomputation would require code change)
RequiresProductDecision: Yes - decide whether simple-average is acceptable as-is or should be weighted

Finding: Future-dated FailureRecord.FailureDate values are not excluded from the MTBF span calculation; ReliabilityDataQualityService tracks other data-quality conditions but this audit found no evidence that future-dated failures are excluded from ReliabilityService's own MTBF calculation.
Evidence: Confirmed by code read of GetEquipmentReliabilityAsync - no date-sanity filter beyond IsActive=1 and EquipmentId match is applied before taking Min/Max FailureDate.
UserImpact: A single erroneously future-dated FailureRecord could distort MTBF (e.g., artificially widen or narrow the calendar span) without any on-screen warning.
AnalyticsImpact: Distorts the per-equipment MTBF value feeding into Availability and Bad Actor's displayed MTBFHours (reused from EquipmentReliabilityDto).
RecommendedAction: Exclude (or flag) FailureRecord.FailureDate values later than the current date from the MTBF span calculation.

Finding: Equipment with zero FailureRecords never appears in GetFleetReliabilityAsync's result at all - the list is built by starting from FailureRecords, not from the Equipment register - so a user cannot distinguish 'no failure history' from 'equipment excluded from this query' without cross-checking the Equipment register separately.
Evidence: Confirmed by code read - the fleet query's starting point is the FailureRecords table
AnalyticsImpact: A newly commissioned or simply reliable piece of equipment is silently absent from the Reliability list rather than shown with zero/null metrics, which could be misread as 'the equipment isn't tracked' rather than 'it has no failures yet.'
DataIntegrityImpact: No incorrect values are produced; this is a completeness/discoverability gap in what the list represents, not a calculation error.
RecommendedAction: None currently - a user must separately check the Equipment register to confirm an equipment's absence means 'no failures,' not 'not tracked.'
RequiresCodeChange: Consider including all equipment (optionally with a filter to show only those with failure history) so absence is not ambiguous, or clearly document that the list is failure-history-driven, not equipment-register-driven.
RequiresSchemaChange: Optional (a Help-content clarification is a non-code fix; changing the list's base query would require code change)
Status: Yes - decide whether the list's scope should change or only be documented
